item.research_question: How does increasing compositional complexity and specific alloying elements in additively manufactured refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) affect helium bubble size, density, and distribution under high-energy helium irradiation compared to pure tungsten?
item.material_system: NbTa, MoNbTa, MoNbTaW, NbTaVW (additively manufactured RHEAs) and pure W (commercial rolled sheet)
item.processing_route: Laser beam directed energy deposition (LB-DED) using elemental Mo, Nb, Ta, V, and W powders; laser powers ranged from 400–750 W (NbTa), 220–350 W (MoNbTa), 1800 W (MoNbTaW), and 800–1000 W (NbTaVW); laser scan velocities 300–600 mm/min; layer thickness 250 µm; substrates preheated to 200–300 °C for NbTa and NbTaVW; pure W was a 2 mm thick rolled sheet cut into 5 mm discs
item.test_conditions: 200 keV He+ ion bombardment at 900 °C to a fluence of 1 × 10^17 cm^-2 at a flux of ~3 × 10^13 cm^-2 s^-1
key_findings: As compositional complexity increased from MoNb to MoNbTa to MoNbTaW, the average He bubble size decreased while the areal density increased.
The NbTaVW RHEA exhibited the largest He bubble diameters (13 nm) compared to the MoNbTaW RHEA (1 nm) due to V segregation.
The pure W control sample had the smallest average bubble diameter (5 nm) and smallest grain size (275 nm), with bubbles accumulating at grain boundaries.
In the NbTaVW sample, V segregation occurred in intercellular/interdendritic regions, and He bubbles accumulated specifically at these V-rich regions.
The average grain size of the NbTaVW sample was ~24 µm, approximately 100 times larger than the W control sample.
No irradiation-induced surface nanofeatures were observed on the SEM scale for any sample following He implantation.
The areal number density of bubbles showed an inverse relationship to size: as bubbles grew larger, their density decreased.
item.mechanism: Increasing compositional complexity and entropy generally limits He bubble size, likely due to lattice distortion effects and changes in melting temperature and elastic modulus. However, the addition of V leads to segregation during AM processing; V has the lowest melting point and lowest binding energy of He to a vacancy, allowing rapid He accumulation into larger bubbles. The net flux of vacancies towards bubbles and larger atoms (Nb, Ta, W) away from bubbles results in V enrichment at the bubbles. Grain boundaries in pure W act as sinks, limiting intragranular bubble size, whereas the large grains in AM RHEAs allow for larger bubbles unless compositional complexity is optimized.
item.limitations: The study notes that the RHEAs have much larger grain sizes (10s of µm) compared to the commercial W (300 nm), which significantly influences bubble density and size; the lack of post-fabrication grain refinement in the AM alloys may mask their full potential. Additionally, the study only investigated He irradiation and did not assess fracture properties, recrystallization performance, or high-temperature mechanical behavior.
item.future_work: Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Further exploration is needed on how post-fabrication treatments to reduce grain sizes could improve bubble characteristics, and the performance of these alloys in other reactor-relevant areas like fracture properties.
quotes: As the RHEA complexity increases from MoNb, to MoNbTa, to MoNbTaW, the He bubble size decreases, while the density increases.
The NbTaVW sample showed larger He bubble diameters than the MoNbTaW sample (13 nm vs. 1 nm), attributed to the substitution of V for Mo.
V atoms are the smallest of the four constituent elements; therefore, the segregation of the other elements is not expected.
